title: A Declared World Model: Language Models Write the Rules of the Scene They Are Shown
content: LeCun’s architecture for autonomous machine intelligence places a learned joint-embedding predictive world model at its centre. We keep its six modules with two departures: the world model is declared rather than learned, and a language model serves as configurator. The configurator writes the rules of the world from a labelled scene graph, and a deterministic engine runs them, accepting or refusing each proposed action; every recovered world is scored against an exact answer key. We ask whether the rules are written for the world or for the picture. From one scene, every configurator tested writes correct rules bound to the objects and numbers in view, and no correct world holds on a layout with a second door. Separating rules from facts, asking for rules over kinds of objects (which lifts only the strongest models), or showing the same world under several layouts lifts the rules over kinds of objects; variation lifts exactly the factors that vary, the doors when the doors vary and the wall when the wall varies, in line with the sufficient-variation condition for learned representations. Because the world model is declared, what each rule is bound to can be read from its text and checked before the world is used.
